arXiv:1210.6526v2 [nlin.SI] 05 Apr 2013

Global existence of small-norm solutions
in the reduced Ostrovsky equation

Roger Grimshaw

Department of Mathematical Sciences, Loughborough University,

Loughborough, LE11 3TU, UK

Dmitry Pelinovsky

Department of Mathematics, McMaster University,

Hamilton, Ontario, L8S 4K1, Canada

Abstract: We use a novel transformation of the reduced Ostrovsky equation to the integrable Tzitzéica equation and prove global existence of small-norm solutions in Sobolev space H3​(ℝ)H^{3}(\mathbb{R}). This scenario is an alternative to finite-time wave breaking of large-norm solutions of the reduced Ostrovsky equation. We also discuss a sharp sufficient condition for the finite-time wave breaking.

1 Introduction

The reduced Ostrovsky equation

(ut+u​ux)x=u,(u_{t}+uu_{x})_{x}=u, (1)

is the zero high-frequency dispersion limit (β→0\beta\to 0) of the Ostrovsky equation

(ut+u​ux+β​ux​x​x)x=u.\left(u_{t}+uu_{x}+\beta u_{xxx}\right)_{x}=u. (2)

The evolution equation (2) was originally derived by Ostrovsky [17] to model small-amplitude long waves in a rotating fluid of finite depth. Local and global well-posedness of the Ostrovsky equation (2) in energy space H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) was studied in recent papers [10, 12, 21, 26].

Corresponding rigorous results for the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) are more complicated. Local solutions exist in Sobolev space Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>32s>\frac{3}{2} [20]. But for sufficiently steep initial data u0∈C1​(ℝ)u_{0}\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}), local solutions break in a finite time [2, 8, 14] in the standard sense of finite-time wave breaking that occurs in the inviscid Burgers equation ut+u​ux=0u_{t}+uu_{x}=0.

However, a proof of global existence for sufficiently small initial data has remained an open problem up to now. In a similar equation with a cubic nonlinear term (called the short-pulse equation), the proof of global existence was recently developed with the help of a bi-infinite sequence of conserved quantities [18]. These global solutions for small initial data coexist with wave breaking solutions for large initial data [13]. Global existence and scattering of small-norm solutions to zero in the generalized short-pulse equation with quartic and higher-order nonlinear terms follow from the results of [20].

Rather different sufficient conditions on the initial data for wave breaking were obtained recently in [9] on the basis of asymptotic analysis and supporting numerical simulations (similar numerical simulations can be found in [2]). It was conjectured in [9] that initial data u0∈C2​(ℝ)u_{0}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}) with 1−3​u0′′​(x)>01-3u^{\prime\prime}_{0}(x)>0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} generate global solutions of the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1), whereas a sign change of this function on the real line inevitably leads to wave breaking in finite time.

This paper is devoted to the rigorous proof of the first part of this conjecture, that is, global solutions exist for all initial data u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) such that 1−3​u0′′​(x)>01-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x)>0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Note here that if u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}), then u0∈C2​(ℝ)u_{0}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}), hence the function 1−3​u0′′​(x)1-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x) is continuous for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and approaches 11 as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty. The second part of the conjecture is also discussed and a weaker statement in line with this conjecture is proven.

Integrability of the reduced Ostrovsky equation was discovered first by Vakhnenko [23]. In a series of papers [16, 24, 25], Vakhnenko, Parkes and collaborators found and explored a transformation of the reduced Ostrovsky equation to the integrable Hirota–Satsuma equation with reversed roles of the variables xx and tt. As a particular application of the power series expansions [19], one can generate a hierarchy of conserved quantities for the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1). This hierarchy includes the first two conserved quantities

E0=∫ℝu2​𝑑x,E−1=∫ℝ[(∂x−1u)2+13​u3]​𝑑x,E_{0}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}u^{2}dx,\quad E_{-1}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left[(\partial_{x}^{-1}u)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}u^{3}\right]dx, (3)

where the anti-derivative operator is defined by the integration of u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) in xx subject to the zero-mass constraint ∫ℝu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x=0\int_{\mathbb{R}}u(x,t)dx=0.

Higher-order conserved quantities E−1E_{-1}, E−2E_{-2}, and so on involve higher-order anti-derivatives, which are defined under additional constraints on the solution uu. Hence, these conserved quantities are not related to the HsH^{s}-norms for positive ss and play no role in the study of global well-posedness of the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) in Sobolev space Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>32s>\frac{3}{2}. Note in passing that the global well-posedness of the regular Hirota–Satsuma equation in the energy space H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) was considered recently in [6].

However, a different transformation has recently been discovered for the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1). This transformation is useful to generate a bi-infinite sequence of conserved quantities, which are more suitable for the proof of global existence.

The alternative formulation of the integrability scheme for the reduced Ostrovsky equation starts with the work of Hone and Wang [7], where the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) was obtained as a short-wave limit of the integrable Degasperis–Procesi equation. As a result of the asymptotic reduction, these authors obtained the following Lax operator pair for the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) in the original space and time variables:

{3​λ​ψx​x​x+(1−3​ux​x)​ψ=0,ψt+λ​ψx​x+u​ψx−ux​ψ=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}3\lambda\psi_{xxx}+(1-3u_{xx})\psi=0,\\ \psi_{t}+\lambda\psi_{xx}+u\psi_{x}-u_{x}\psi=0,\end{array}\right. (4)

where λ\lambda is a spectral parameter. Note that the function 1−3​ux​x1-3u_{xx} arises naturally in the third-order eigenvalue problem (4) in the same way as the function m=u−ux​xm=u-u_{xx} arises in another integrable Camassa–Holm equation to determine if the global solutions or wave breaking will occur in the Cauchy problem [4, 5].

More recently, based on an earlier study of Manna & Neveu [15], Kraenkel et al. [11] found a transformation between the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) and the integrable Bullough–Dodd equation, which is also widely known as the Tzitzéica equation after its original derivation in 1910 [22]. In new characteristic variables YY and TT (see section 2), the Tzitzéica equation can be written in the form,

∂2V∂T​∂Y=e−2​V−eV.\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial T\partial Y}=e^{-2V}-e^{V}. (5)

Note that the Tzitzéica equation is similar to the sine–Gordon equation in characteristic coordinates, which arises in the integrability scheme of the short-pulse equation [18]. Similarly to the sine–Gordon equation, the Tzitzéica equation has a bi-infinite sequence of conserved quantities, which was discovered in two recent and independent works [1, 3]. Among those, we only need the first two conserved quantities

Q1=∫ℝ(2​eV+e−2​V−3)​𝑑Y,Q2=∫ℝ(∂V∂Y)2​𝑑Y,Q_{1}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(2e^{V}+e^{-2V}-3\right)dY,\quad Q_{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial Y}\right)^{2}dY, (6)

which were obtained from the power series expansions [1]. The conserved quantities (6) are related to the conserved quantities of the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) in original physical variables

E1=∫ℝ[(1−3​ux​x)1/3−1]​𝑑x,E2=∫ℝ(ux​x​x)2(1−3​ux​x)7/3​𝑑x.E_{1}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left[\left(1-3u_{xx}\right)^{1/3}-1\right]dx,\quad E_{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{(u_{xxx})^{2}}{(1-3u_{xx})^{7/3}}dx. (7)

Note that the conserved quantities (7) also appeared in the balance equations derived in [11].

In Section 2, we shall use the conserved quantities E0E_{0} in (3) and Q1Q_{1}, Q2Q_{2} in (6), as well as the reduction to the Tzitzéica equation (5), to prove our main result, which is,

Theorem 1

Assume u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) such that 1−3​u0′′​(x)>01-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x)>0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Then, the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) admits a unique global solution u∈C⁡(ℝ+,H3​(ℝ))u\in C(\mathbb{R}_{+},H^{3}(\mathbb{R})).

It is natural to expect that the finite-time wave breaking occurs for any u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) such that 1−3​u0′′​(x)1-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x) changes sign for some x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. As shown in [9] in a periodic setting, this criterion of wave breaking is sharper than the previous criteria of wave breaking in [8, 14]. Although we are not able to give a full proof of this sharp criterion in the present work, we shall prove the following weaker statement in Section 3:

Theorem 2

Assume that u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) is given and there is a finite interval [X−,X+][X_{-},X_{+}] and a point X0∈(X−,X+)X_{0}\in(X_{-},X_{+}) such that

1−3​u0′′​(x)<0,x∈(X−,X+),1-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x)<0,\quad x\in(X_{-},X_{+}), (8)

and

u0′​(x)<0,x∈(X−,X0),u0′​(x)>0,x∈(X0,X+),u_{0}^{\prime}(x)<0,\quad x\in(X_{-},X_{0}),\qquad u_{0}^{\prime}(x)>0,\quad x\in(X_{0},X_{+}), (9)

whereas 1−3​u0′′​(x)≥01-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x)\geq 0 for all x≤X−x\leq X_{-} and x≥X+x\geq X_{+}. Then, a local solution u∈C⁡([0,t0),H3​(ℝ))u\in C([0,t_{0}),H^{3}(\mathbb{R})) of the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) breaks in a finite time t0∈(0,∞)t_{0}\in(0,\infty) in the sense

lim supt↑t0‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖H3​(ℝ)=∞\limsup_{t\uparrow t_{0}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{3}(\mathbb{R})}=\infty

if ux​(x−​(t),t)<0u_{x}(x_{-}(t),t)<0 and ux​(x+​(t),t)>0u_{x}(x_{+}(t),t)>0 hold for all t∈[0,t0)t\in[0,t_{0}) along the characteristics x=x±​(t)x=x_{\pm}(t) originating from x±​(0)=X±x_{\pm}(0)=X_{\pm}.

A prototypical example of the initial data for the reduced Ostrovsky equation on the infinite line is the first Hermite function u0​(x)=x​e−a​x2u_{0}(x)=xe^{-ax^{2}}, where a>0a>0 is a parameter. A straightforward computation of the maximum of u0′′​(x)u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x) shows that u0′′​(x)<13u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x)<\frac{1}{3} for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} if a∈(0,a0)a\in(0,a_{0}), where

a0=e3−6108​(3−6)≈0.0292.a_{0}=\frac{e^{3-\sqrt{6}}}{108(3-\sqrt{6})}\approx 0.0292.

In this case, Theorem 1 implies global existence of solutions for such initial data. When a>a0a>a_{0}, condition (8) is satisfied. In addition, u0​(x)u_{0}(x) has a global minimum at x=−12​ax=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}} so that condition (9) is satisfied for a>a∗=e72≈0.0378a>a_{*}=\frac{e}{72}\approx 0.0378. (Note that a∗>a0a_{*}>a_{0}.) Theorem 2 implies wave breaking in a finite time provided that additional constraints are satisfied, that is, ux​(x−​(t),t)<0u_{x}(x_{-}(t),t)<0 and ux​(x+​(t),t)>0u_{x}(x_{+}(t),t)>0 hold for all times before the wave breaking time along the characteristics x=x±​(t)x=x_{\pm}(t) originating from x±​(0)=X±x_{\pm}(0)=X_{\pm}. Although we strongly believe that these additional constraints as well as condition (9) are not needed for the statement of Theorem 2, we were not able to lift out these technical restrictions.

The initial function u0​(x)=x​e−a​x2u_{0}(x)=xe^{-ax^{2}} for a>a∗a>a_{*} is shown on Fig. 1, where the points X−X_{-}, X+X_{+}, and X0X_{0} introduced in Theorem 2 are also shown.

2 Proof of Theorem 1

We introduce characteristic coordinates for the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) [9, 14, 23]:

x=X+∫0TU⁡(X,T′)​d​T′,t=T,u⁡(x,t)=U⁡(X,T).x=X+\int_{0}^{T}U(X,T^{\prime})dT^{\prime},\quad t=T,\quad u(x,t)=U(X,T). (10)

The coordinate tranformation is one-to-one and onto if the Jacobian

ϕ⁡(X,T)=1+∫0TUX​(X,T′)​d​T′,\phi(X,T)=1+\int_{0}^{T}U_{X}(X,T^{\prime})dT^{\prime}, (11)

which is positive for T=0T=0 because ϕ⁡(X,0)=1\phi(X,0)=1, remains positive for all (X,T)∈ℝ×[0,T0](X,T)\in\mathbb{R}\times[0,T_{0}], where T0>0T_{0}>0 is the local existence time.

We note that the original equation (1) yields the relation

u\displaystyle u =\displaystyle= UX​Tϕ=ϕT​Tϕ,\displaystyle\frac{U_{XT}}{\phi}=\frac{\phi_{TT}}{\phi}, (12)

whereas the transformation formulas (10) and (11) yield the relations

ux\displaystyle u_{x} =\displaystyle= UXϕ=ϕTϕ,\displaystyle\frac{U_{X}}{\phi}=\frac{\phi_{T}}{\phi}, (13)

and

ux​x\displaystyle u_{xx} =\displaystyle= 1ϕ​(UXϕ)X=ϕT​X​ϕ−ϕX​ϕTϕ3.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\phi}\left(\frac{U_{X}}{\phi}\right)_{X}=\frac{\phi_{TX}\phi-\phi_{X}\phi_{T}}{\phi^{3}}. (14)

Next, in accordance with [11], we introduce the variable

f=(1−3​ux​x)1/3.f=(1-3u_{xx})^{1/3}\,. (15)

If uu satisfies the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1), then ff satisfies the balance equation

ft+(u​f)x={u−ux​t−(u​ux)x}xf2/3=0.f_{t}+(uf)_{x}=\frac{\{u-u_{xt}-(uu_{x})_{x}\}_{x}}{f^{2/3}}=0\,. (16)

In characteristic coordinates (10), we set f⁡(x,t)=F⁡(X,T)f(x,t)=F(X,T), use equation (13), and rewrite the balance equation (16) in the equivalent form

(F​ϕ)T=0⇒F⁡(X,T)​ϕ​(X,T)=F0​(X),(F\phi)_{T}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad F(X,T)\phi(X,T)=F_{0}(X), (17)

where F0​(X)=F​(X,0)F_{0}(X)=F(X,0). Using equations (14) and (15), we obtain the evolution equation for F⁡(X,T)F(X,T):

∂2∂T​∂X​log⁡(F)=−∂2∂T​∂X​log⁡(ϕ)=13​ϕ​(F3−1)=13​F0​(X)​(F2−F−1).\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial T\partial X}\log(F)=-\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial T\partial X}\log(\phi)=\frac{1}{3}\phi(F^{3}-1)=\frac{1}{3}F_{0}(X)(F^{2}-F^{-1}). (18)

We shall now consider the Cauchy problem for the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) with initial data u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}). By the local well-posedness result [20], there exists a unique local solution of the reduced Ostrovsky equation in class u∈C⁡([0,t0],H3​(ℝ))u\in C([0,t_{0}],H^{3}(\mathbb{R})) for some t0>0t_{0}>0. By Sobolev embedding of H3​(ℝ)H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) into C2​(ℝ)C^{2}(\mathbb{R}), the function f0​(x):=(1−3​u0′′​(x))1/3f_{0}(x):=(1-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x))^{1/3} is continuous, bounded, and satisfies f0​(x)→1f_{0}(x)\to 1 as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty.

To prove Theorem 1, we further require that f0​(x)>0f_{0}(x)>0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, which means from the above properties that infx∈ℝf0​(x)>0\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}f_{0}(x)>0. Because x=Xx=X for t=T=0t=T=0, we have F0∈C⁡(ℝ)F_{0}\in C(\mathbb{R}) such that infX∈ℝF0​(X)>0\inf_{X\in\mathbb{R}}F_{0}(X)>0. In this case, the transformation from XX to YY defined by

Y:=−13∫0XF0(X′)dX′Y:=-\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{X}F_{0}(X^{\prime})dX^{\prime} (19)

We can now transfer the well-posedness result for local solutions of the reduced Ostrovsky equation (1) to local solutions of the Tzitzéica equation (5).

Lemma 1

Assume u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) such that 1−3​u0′′​(x)>01-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x)>0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Let

V0(Y):=−13log(1−3u0′′(x)),Y:=−13∫0x(1−3u0′′(x′))1/3dx′.V_{0}(Y):=-\frac{1}{3}\log(1-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x)),\quad Y:=-\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{x}(1-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(x^{\prime}))^{1/3}dx^{\prime}.

There exists a unique local solution of the Tzitzéica equation (5) in class V∈C⁡([0,T0],H1​(ℝ))V\in C([0,T_{0}],H^{1}(\mathbb{R})) for some T0>0T_{0}>0 such that V​(Y,0)=V0​(Y)V(Y,0)=V_{0}(Y).

ux​x​(x,t)=13​(1−f3​(x,t))=13​(1−e−3​V​(Y,T)).u_{xx}(x,t)=\frac{1}{3}\left(1-f^{3}(x,t)\right)=\frac{1}{3}\left(1-e^{-3V(Y,T)}\right).

G⁡(ux​x):=log⁡(1−3​ux​x)(−3​ux​x).G(u_{xx}):=\frac{\log(1-3u_{xx})}{(-3u_{xx})}.

Remark 1

The Jacobian of the transformation from (X,T)(X,T) to (x,t)(x,t) is given by (11) and controlled by the relation (13). Since ϕ⁡(X,0)=1\phi(X,0)=1 and

ϕ⁡(X,T)=exp⁡(∫0Tux​(x⁡(X,T),T)​𝑑T),\phi(X,T)=\exp\left(\int_{0}^{T}u_{x}(x(X,T),T)dT\right), (21)

we can see that there is T0>0T_{0}>0 such that ϕ⁡(X,T)>0\phi(X,T)>0 for all (X,T)∈ℝ×[0,T0](X,T)\in\mathbb{R}\times[0,T_{0}]. Because

ϕ⁡(X,T)=F0​(X)F⁡(X,T)=F0​(X)​eV⁡(Y,T),\phi(X,T)=\frac{F_{0}(X)}{F(X,T)}=F_{0}(X)e^{V(Y,T)}, (22)

the condition ϕ⁡(X,T)>0\phi(X,T)>0 remains true as long as V⁡(Y,T)V(Y,T) remains bounded in L∞L^{\infty}-norm.

Lemma 2

Let V∈C⁡([0,T0],H1​(ℝ))V\in C([0,T_{0}],H^{1}(\mathbb{R})) for some T0>0T_{0}>0 be a unique local solution of the Tzitzéica equation (5). Then, in fact, V∈C⁡(ℝ+,H1​(ℝ))V\in C(\mathbb{R}_{+},H^{1}(\mathbb{R})).

Proof. We shall use Q1Q_{1} and Q2Q_{2} in (6). The quantities are well-defined for a local solution in class V∈C⁡([0,T0],H1​(ℝ))V\in C([0,T_{0}],H^{1}(\mathbb{R})) and conserves in time for the Tzitzéica equation (5), according to the standard approximation arguments in Sobolev spaces.

To be able to use Q1Q_{1} for the control of ‖V⁡(⋅,T)‖L2\|V(\cdot,T)\|_{L^{2}}, we note that the function H⁡(V):=2​eV+e−2​V−3H(V):=2e^{V}+e^{-2V}-3 is convex near V=0V=0 with H⁡(0)=H′​(0)=0H(0)=H^{\prime}(0)=0 and

H′′​(V)=2​eV+4​e−2​V≥2,V∈ℝ.H^{\prime\prime}(V)=2e^{V}+4e^{-2V}\geq 2,\quad V\in\mathbb{R}.

‖V‖H12=‖V‖L22+‖VY‖L22≤Q1+Q2.\|V\|_{H^{1}}^{2}=\|V\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|V_{Y}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq Q_{1}+Q_{2}.

By a standard continuation technique, a local solution in class V∈C⁡([0,T0],H1​(ℝ))V\in C([0,T_{0}],H^{1}(\mathbb{R})) is uniquely continued into a global solution in class V∈C⁡(ℝ+,H1​(ℝ))V\in C(\mathbb{R}_{+},H^{1}(\mathbb{R})). □\Box

It remains to transfer results of Lemmas 1 and 2, as well as the L2L^{2} conservation of E0E_{0} in (3) for the proof of Theorem 1.

Proof of Theorem 1. It follows from the proof in Lemma 1 that ux​x=V​g​(V)u_{xx}=Vg(V), where

g⁡(V):=1−e−3​V3​V.g(V):=\frac{1-e^{-3V}}{3V}.

Therefore, ϕ⁡(X,T)>0\phi(X,T)>0 for all (X,T)∈ℝ×ℝ+(X,T)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}, so that the transformation (10) is one-to-one and onto for all (X,T)∈ℝ×ℝ+(X,T)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}. Using the bounded functions gg and g′g^{\prime}, we hence have ux​x∈C⁡(ℝ+,H1​(ℝ))u_{xx}\in C(\mathbb{R}_{+},H^{1}(\mathbb{R})).

Finally, conservation of E0E_{0} in (3) and the elementary Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

‖ux‖L22≤‖u‖L2​‖ux​x‖L2,\|u_{x}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\|u\|_{L^{2}}\|u_{xx}\|_{L^{2}},

implies that u∈C⁡(ℝ+,H3​(ℝ))u\in C(\mathbb{R}_{+},H^{3}(\mathbb{R})). This argument completes the proof of Theorem 1. □\Box

3 Proof of Theorem 2

We utilize the characteristic coordinates (10) and consider the evolution of the Jacobian ϕ\phi defined by (11). Recall that ϕ⁡(X,0)=1\phi(X,0)=1 whereas F⁡(X,0)=F0​(X)=(1−3​u0′′​(X))1/3F(X,0)=F_{0}(X)=(1-3u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(X))^{1/3}. Using conservation (17) and evolution (18) for FF, we obtain the evolution equation for ϕ⁡(X,T)\phi(X,T):

Integrating this equation in TT with the initial condition ϕ⁡(X,0)=1\phi(X,0)=1, we obtain

∂ϕ∂X=13​ϕ​(X,T)​∫0Tϕ⁡(X,T′)​(1−F03​(X)ϕ3​(X,T′))​d​T′.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial X}=\frac{1}{3}\phi(X,T)\int_{0}^{T}\phi(X,T^{\prime})\left(1-\frac{F_{0}^{3}(X)}{\phi^{3}(X,T^{\prime})}\right)dT^{\prime}. (24)

Lemma 3

Let ψ⁡(X,T):=∫0Tϕ⁡(X,T′)​d​T′\psi(X,T):=\int_{0}^{T}\phi(X,T^{\prime})dT^{\prime}. Under assumption (8) of Theorem 2, we have

∂ψ∂X≥16​ψ2​(X,T),X∈(X−,X+),\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial X}\geq\frac{1}{6}\psi^{2}(X,T),\quad X\in(X_{-},X_{+}), (25)

as long as the solution remains in class u∈C⁡([0,t0],H3​(ℝ))u\in C([0,t_{0}],H^{3}(\mathbb{R})).

Proof. Because F0​(X)<0F_{0}(X)<0 for all X∈(X−,X+)X\in(X_{-},X_{+}), we have from (24):

∂ϕ∂X≥13​ϕ​(X,T)​∫0Tϕ⁡(X,T′)​d​T′=16​∂∂T​(∫0Tϕ⁡(X,T′)​d​T′)2.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial X}\geq\frac{1}{3}\phi(X,T)\int_{0}^{T}\phi(X,T^{\prime})dT^{\prime}=\frac{1}{6}\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left(\int_{0}^{T}\phi(X,T^{\prime})dT^{\prime}\right)^{2}.

It follows from Lemma 3 that

Lemma 4

Under assumptions (8) and (9) of Theorem 2, there exists a C1C^{1} function ξ⁡(T)\xi(T) and TT-independent constants ξ±\xi_{\pm} such that ϕ⁡(ξ⁡(T),T)=1\phi(\xi(T),T)=1, ξ⁡(0)=X0∈(X−,X+)\xi(0)=X_{0}\in(X_{-},X_{+}), and ξ⁡(T)∈[ξ−,ξ+]⊂(X−,X+)\xi(T)\in[\xi_{-},\xi_{+}]\subset(X_{-},X_{+}) for all T≥0T\geq 0, as long as the solution remains in class u∈C⁡([0,t0],H3​(ℝ))u\in C([0,t_{0}],H^{3}(\mathbb{R})) with UX​(X−,T)<0U_{X}(X_{-},T)<0 and UX​(X+,T)>0U_{X}(X_{+},T)>0.

Remark 2

Since ξ⁡(0)=X0\xi(0)=X_{0} is the point of minimum of U​(X,0)=u0​(X)U(X,0)=u_{0}(X) and ϕX​(X,0)=0\phi_{X}(X,0)=0, it follows from equation (27) that

ξ′​(0)=−UX​T​(X0,0)+ξ′​(0)​UX​X​(X0,0)ϕX​T​(X0,T)⇒ξ′​(0)=−u0​(X0)2​u0′′​(X0).\xi^{\prime}(0)=-\frac{U_{XT}(X_{0},0)+\xi^{\prime}(0)U_{XX}(X_{0},0)}{\phi_{XT}(X_{0},T)}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\xi^{\prime}(0)=-\frac{u_{0}(X_{0})}{2u_{0}^{\prime\prime}(X_{0})}.

This equation shows that ξ′​(0)>0\xi^{\prime}(0)>0 if u0​(X0)<0u_{0}(X_{0})<0 and ξ′​(0)<0\xi^{\prime}(0)<0 if u0​(X0)>0u_{0}(X_{0})>0. Remark 3

Based on the asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations of [9], we anticipate that divergence of ϕ⁡(X,T)\phi(X,T) near X=X+X=X_{+} is related to the vanishing of ϕ⁡(X,T)\phi(X,T) near X=X−X=X_{-}, such that equation (13) with UX​(X−,T)<0U_{X}(X_{-},T)<0 would imply that uxu_{x} diverges in a finite time near x=x−​(t)x=x_{-}(t).
